name: eKuiper
vendor: LF Edge (Linux Foundation), started at EMQ
summary: A small stream processing engine for edge gateways: SQL rules filter, window and aggregate sensor data from MQTT, EdgeX and other sources before it leaves the site.
intro: Sending every raw sensor reading to the cloud costs bandwidth and adds latency, and a gateway beside the machines usually has a few hundred megabytes of memory, not a Flink cluster. eKuiper is a single Go binary for that gateway: the core server package is about 4.5 MB and uses about 10 MB of memory, and it runs on x86 and Arm, 32- and 64-bit, on Linux distributions including OpenWrt, on macOS and in Docker. Its own README calls it a streaming framework “similar to Apache Flink” at the edge.

You first declare a stream, which works like a table definition: a schema, a format such as JSON, and a source, for example an MQTT topic filter. A rule is then a SQL query over streams, or a graph of nodes in the style of Node-RED, plus a list of actions that say where results go. The SQL has more than 60 functions, joins with tables and lookups in databases, and four time windows plus a count window. Built-in sources include MQTT, EdgeX, Neuron, HTTP, files, Redis and WebSocket, with plug-ins for SQL databases, Kafka, ZeroMQ and video; sinks add InfluxDB, IoTDB and others. Sources, sinks and functions can be extended in Go or Python, including functions that run ONNX models. Rules are managed through a CLI, a REST API, a web dashboard or Kubernetes config maps.

State such as an open window lives in memory by default. Setting a rule’s `qos` to 1 or 2 turns on checkpointing to storage, giving at-least-once or exactly-once effects on that state after a crash, provided the source can rewind; the sink can still receive duplicates. eKuiper is the rules engine the EdgeX Foundry docs list among their supporting services. EMQ, which created it, open-sourced it in 2019 and donated it to LF Edge in 2021, where it sits at the At-Large stage; the 2.x series began in October 2024, and 2.4.0 followed in May 2026.
strengths: Very small: about 4.5 MB on disk and 10 MB of memory, so it fits on industrial gateways, routers and Raspberry Pi-class boards
Rules are SQL with windows, joins and 60+ functions, so filtering and aggregating at the edge doesn’t need custom code
Ready-made connectors for MQTT, EdgeX and the Neuron industrial gateway, with plug-ins for Kafka, SQL databases and time-series stores
Rules can be added, changed and stopped at runtime through a REST API, which suits gateways managed remotely
limits: One process on one machine: there is no cluster or partitioning, so it doesn’t scale out like Flink or Kafka Streams
State is in memory unless checkpointing is turned on, and even then exactly once only covers internal state, not what the sinks receive
An At-Large LF Edge project, the entry stage, and closely tied to EMQ, which integrates it with its own EMQX, Neuron and NanoMQ products
Many connectors, including Kafka and SQL, are plug-ins that have to be built or installed separately

snippet.title: A rule: every 5 seconds, publish the averages if it got hot
source: "sql": "SELECT count(*), avg(temperature) as avg_temp, max(humidity) as max_hum from demo group by TUMBLINGWINDOW(ss, 5) HAVING avg_temp > 30;",

story: EMQ, the company behind the EMQX MQTT broker, wrote Kuiper for places such as production lines, connected vehicles and wind farms, where processing device data on the gateway cuts latency, bandwidth and storage costs. Stream processors such as Flink were built for clusters, so Kuiper was a small Go engine with a SQL rule language. EMQ open-sourced it in 2019, and its first release, 0.0.2, came that October with `SELECT … FROM … WHERE`, functions and a command-line tool.

Integration with EdgeX Foundry came early: version 0.3.2, in April 2020, was the release that shipped with EdgeX’s Geneva release, and eKuiper went on to become the rules engine in the EdgeX documentation. Version 1.0.0 followed in October 2020. In April 2021 the project was put to the LF Edge Technical Advisory Council for the At-Large stage, and it was donated to LF Edge that year under the name LF Edge eKuiper.

Releases came roughly every quarter after that. Version 2.0 in October 2024 reworked connections so several rules share one, split sources and sinks into separately measured steps, added an ONNX function for running models, and added OpenTelemetry tracing.

choices.why: Plant engineers and integrators already knew SQL, and a declarative query can be added or changed on a running gateway without compiling anything.

choices.choice: A single small binary in Go
choices.why: Edge gateways have little memory and many CPU architectures; a static Go binary of a few megabytes runs on all of them without a JVM.

choices.choice: Plug-ins for everything beyond the basics
choices.why: Keeping Kafka, SQL and video connectors out of the core keeps the default build small for devices that only need MQTT.
